title: Making Every Contact Count and behaviour change
blurb: Use routine contacts for brief health conversations: smoking VBA, alcohol units, activity, and matching support to motivation.
question: While redressing a leg ulcer, a community nurse learns that Mr Pereira, 59, smokes 15 cigarettes a day, drinks about 30 units a week and rarely leaves the house. He says, 'I know, I know.' With five minutes left, what should the nurse do?

teach.h: What Making Every Contact Count is
teach.body: MECC is an approach to behaviour change that uses the millions of day-to-day interactions that organisations and people have with others to support them in making positive changes to their physical and mental health and wellbeing. In plain English: every routine contact is a chance for a short, consistent health conversation, without adding a separate appointment. Proficiency P2.4 asks nurses to use these opportunities, with reasonable adjustments, to discuss smoking, alcohol and substance use, sexual behaviours, diet and exercise.
teach.cite: NHS England et al., MECC consensus statement (2016)

rows.label: Time
values: 30 seconds to a couple of minutes

teach.caption: NICE PH49 also describes extended brief interventions (more than 30 minutes) and high intensity interventions.

letters.word: Ask: establish and record smoking status
Advise: best way to stop is medication plus specialist support
Act: offer referral to local stop smoking support

teach.caption: NCSCT Very Brief Advice takes about 30 seconds. Unlike a longer consultation, it does not explore motivation first, so it suits every person who smokes (NICE NG209 supports VBA).

items.label: per week, men and women: low-risk alcohol limit
spread drinking over, with drink-free days
moderate activity a week (or 75 min vigorous)

teach.caption: UK CMOs' low risk drinking guidelines (2016); UK CMOs' physical activity guidelines (2019). In pregnancy the safest approach is not to drink.

items: One UK unit is 10 mL of pure alcohol.
Units = (ABV % × volume in mL) ÷ 1,000.
Example: a 250 mL glass of 12% wine = 12 × 250 ÷ 1,000 = 3 units.
Example: a pint (568 mL) of 5% lager = 5 × 568 ÷ 1,000 = 2.8 units.
Check: six pints of 4% beer = 6 × (4 × 568 ÷ 1,000) = about 13.6 units, just under the weekly limit.

teach.h: Assess motivation, then match the support
teach.body: NICE PH49 asks practitioners to assess a person's capability, opportunity and motivation (the COM-B model) and, where several behaviours need to change, which one the person is most motivated to tackle. Effective support includes agreeing goals and plans, self-monitoring with feedback, and social support. Relapse is common: plan for it with coping and 'if-then' plans, and keep follow-up going for at least a year after an intervention.
teach.cite: NICE PH49 Behaviour change: individual approaches (2014) recs 8–10

teach.h: Where to start when several behaviours need to change

children.label: Which one matters most to you?
Agree one goal and a plan
Brief advice, leave the door open

teach.body: District nurse Hana uses the last five minutes of the dressing visit. Ask: she confirms he smokes 15 a day. Advise: 'The best way to stop is with stop smoking medication plus support from a specialist service.' Act: he agrees to a referral. She asks which change matters most to him; he says walking to the corner shop again. They set a goal of a walk around the block twice this week, which he will tick off on his calendar. She notes alcohol for the next visit.

teach.text: Don't wait for someone to say they are ready before giving smoking VBA: Ask, Advise, Act is offered to everyone who smokes. And don't confuse MECC Level 1 (very brief, 30 seconds to a couple of minutes) with an extended brief intervention (more than 30 minutes).

items: MECC uses everyday contacts for brief, consistent health conversations, with reasonable adjustments.
Level 1 very brief: 30 seconds to a couple of minutes. Level 2 brief: discussion, negotiation, encouragement.
Smoking VBA: Ask, Advise (medication plus specialist support), Act (refer).
Alcohol: no more than 14 units a week, spread over 3 or more days; 1 unit = 10 mL pure alcohol.
Activity: 150 min moderate or 75 min vigorous a week, plus strength on 2 days; break up sitting.
Assess motivation (COM-B); start with the behaviour the person most wants to change; plan for relapse.

summary: You can now use routine contacts for very brief and brief interventions, deliver smoking Very Brief Advice and calculate alcohol units against the 14-unit guideline. You can also assess motivation and agree realistic, self-monitored goals that plan for relapse.

A.q: What are the three steps of Very Brief Advice on smoking?
A.why: NCSCT Very Brief Advice: Ask about and record smoking status, Advise on the best way to stop, Act by offering referral to stop smoking support.

whyNot.0: This resembles older '5 As' wording, not the three VBA steps.
whyNot.1: 'Arrange' is part of the 5 As model; VBA's third step is Act.
whyNot.3: VBA starts by asking, not assessing, and has no 'agree' step.

A.q: Under the UK Chief Medical Officers' 2016 guidelines, what is the low-risk weekly alcohol limit for men?
A.why: UK CMOs (2016): to keep health risks low, men and women are advised not to drink more than 14 units a week on a regular basis.

whyNot.0: 10 units is not the guideline figure.
whyNot.1: 21 units was the old weekly figure for men, replaced in 2016.
whyNot.2: 28 units is double the current guideline.

A.q: A healthcare assistant spends about a minute at a blood test appointment giving information on a local walking group. Which MECC level is this?
A.why: MECC Level 1, very brief intervention, takes 30 seconds to a couple of minutes and gives information or signposts to further help (MECC consensus 2016).

whyNot.0: A brief intervention involves discussion, negotiation or encouragement, usually a few minutes.
whyNot.1: Extended brief interventions last more than 30 minutes (NICE PH49).
whyNot.3: High intensity interventions are longer programmes for people at high risk.

B.q: Mr Holt, 63, drinks four 440 mL cans of 5% lager each week. How many units is this?
B.why: Each can: 5 × 440 ÷ 1,000 = 2.2 units. Four cans = 8.8 units a week, within the 14-unit guideline.

whyNot.0: 4.4 units is two cans, not four.
whyNot.3: 17.6 units doubles the correct figure, as if each can held 4.4 units.

B.q: Siobhan, 44, drinks nothing from Sunday to Thursday, then about 6 units on Friday night and 8 units on Saturday night. What is the most accurate advice?
options: Her total is within guidance, so no change is needed
She should switch to spirits to reduce the volume
Two drinking days a week is the recommended pattern
Spread it over 3 or more days, with drink-free days
B.why: UK CMOs (2016): if drinking up to 14 units a week, spread it evenly over 3 or more days; heavy drinking episodes increase risks. Several drink-free days are a good way to cut down.

whyNot.0: Her weekly total is 14 units, but drinking it over two heavy sessions increases risk.
whyNot.1: Switching drink type does not change the alcohol in units or the risk of heavy episodes.
whyNot.2: The guidance is to spread drinking over 3 or more days.

B.q: Mr Adebayo, 61, has type 2 diabetes. He smokes, eats takeaways most evenings and rarely exercises. At his review he sighs, 'I want to sort myself out, but where do I even start?' What is the best next step?
options: Ask him which change he feels most motivated to make
Give him a plan to tackle all three behaviours at once
Start with smoking, as it carries the highest risk
Postpone the discussion to his next annual review
B.why: NICE PH49: assess motivation and, if many behaviours need to change, which one the person is most motivated to tackle. Starting there builds confidence.

whyNot.1: Tackling everything at once is likely to feel more overwhelming.
whyNot.2: The nurse choosing the priority ignores his motivation, which predicts success.
whyNot.3: He has asked for help now; postponing for a year misses the opportunity.

C.q: Priya, 45, cut out drinking on weeknights two months ago. She is anxious that her work Christmas party will undo her progress. Which approach from NICE PH49 is most useful?
options: Tell her that one night of drinking will not matter
Help her make an 'if-then' plan for the party
Advise her to skip the party to remove the risk
Reassure her that relapse is rare after two months
C.why: NICE PH49: relapse is common; people should have well-rehearsed action plans such as 'if-then' plans they can use if tempted or if they slip.

whyNot.0: Downplaying a lapse can trigger full relapse.
whyNot.2: Avoiding social events is not realistic or person-centred; planning is.
whyNot.3: Relapse is common, which is why NICE stresses planning for it.

C.q: Joan, 70, wants to stay independent. She walks slowly for 20 minutes most days. Under the UK CMOs' guidelines, what else should the nurse encourage?
options: Stopping walking as it is too low in intensity to help
Running 75 minutes a week instead of walking
Strength and balance activities on 2 days a week
Resting more to save energy for daily tasks
C.why: UK CMOs (2019): older adults should do activities to improve or maintain muscle strength, balance and flexibility on at least 2 days a week, aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity, and break up sitting.

whyNot.0: Some activity is better than none; even light activity benefits older adults.
whyNot.1: Vigorous activity is an option for those already active, but strength and balance are the key gap here.
whyNot.3: More sedentary time increases risk; the guidance is to break up sitting.

C.q: A nurse delivers smoking VBA to Mr Ibe, who says, 'I'm not ready to quit.' What should the nurse do?
options: Record that he declined and stop the conversation
Repeat the health risks until he agrees to a referral
Refer him to the stop smoking service without his agreement
Note his answer and keep the offer of support open
C.why: VBA is offered to everyone; if the person does not want support now, record it and make clear help is available whenever he wants it, revisiting at future contacts.

whyNot.0: Closing the topic misses the chance to keep the door open for later.

reteach.title: Thirty seconds that matter
reteach.question: If you had only thirty seconds with a patient who smokes, what would you say?

blocks.body: ASK: 'Do you smoke?' and record it. ADVISE: 'The best way to stop is with stop smoking medicine and support from a specialist service.' ACT: 'I can refer you today.' The same habit works for other topics: notice an opportunity, give one clear message, point to help.

blocks.text: The 14-unit guideline is the same for men and women since 2016.

explain.body: Uses day-to-day interactions to support positive changes to physical and mental health and wellbeing. Level 1: 30 seconds to a couple of minutes. Level 2: brief discussion, negotiation, encouragement.

items: Opportunistic
Consistent message
Signpost or refer

test.q: How long does a MECC Level 1 very brief intervention typically take?
options: 30 seconds to a couple of minutes
test.why: MECC consensus statement (2016): a very brief intervention can take from 30 seconds to a couple of minutes.

whyNot.0: 10 to 15 minutes is longer than a very brief intervention.
whyNot.2: More than 30 minutes is an extended brief intervention.
whyNot.3: An hour describes a longer, more intensive session.

explain.body: 1 unit = 10 mL pure alcohol. Units = ABV% × mL ÷ 1,000. Low-risk: no more than 14 units a week, spread over 3+ days, several drink-free days. Pregnancy: safest not to drink.

test.q: How many units are in a 500 mL can of 8% cider?

whyNot.0: 2 units would be a 500 mL drink at 4% ABV.
whyNot.2: 6 units would need 12% ABV at this volume.
whyNot.3: 8 units confuses the ABV with the unit count.

explain.body: Adults: at least 150 minutes moderate or 75 minutes vigorous activity a week, strength on at least 2 days, minimise sitting. Older adults also include balance and flexibility on 2 days.

test.q: What weekly amount of moderate intensity activity do the UK CMOs recommend for adults?
test.why: UK CMOs (2019): at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity activity a week, or 75 minutes vigorous.

whyNot.0: 60 minutes a day is the children's guideline, not the adult weekly figure.

explain.body: Assess capability, opportunity and motivation (COM-B). Start with the behaviour the person most wants to change. Agree goals, self-monitor, give feedback, build social support. Plan for relapse with if-then plans.

items: Skills
Knowledge

items: Wanting
Habits

test.q: In the COM-B model used by NICE PH49, what do the three letters C, O and M stand for?
test.why: COM-B: behaviour depends on capability, opportunity and motivation (NICE PH49).

whyNot.1: These words relate to behaviour change but are not the COM-B components.
whyNot.2: These are not the COM-B components.
whyNot.3: Capacity is a legal concept; these are not the COM-B components.
